items.title: Each of your sperm/eggs is one of 2 to the 23rd power possibilities
items.claim: Meiosis shuffles 23 chromosome pairs into 23 gametes. From you alone, ignoring recombination, that's 8.4 million possible combinations. Add crossing over and the count is effectively infinite. Why is sexual reproduction so expensive to maintain?
items.prompt: Why has sex (rather than cloning) persisted in almost all eukaryotes?

options.text: Sex is uniformly better than cloning

Sex generates genetic variation that helps populations adapt to changing environments (the Red Queen hypothesis: ongoing host-parasite arms races favour variability); also recombination weeds out accumulated harmful mutations more efficiently than clonal lineages can
Sex is necessary for cell division

items.reveal_title: The twofold cost and the Red Queen
items.reveal:
A sexually reproducing female passes 50 percent of her genes to each offspring. An asexual female passes 100 percent. Asexual lineages should outcompete sexual ones by a factor of two each generation. They mostly don't.

Leading explanations:
- Red Queen (Hamilton, Van Valen): parasites and pathogens evolve to attack common host genotypes; sexual reproduction keeps host genotypes shifting so parasites can't catch up.
- Muller's ratchet: asexual lineages accumulate harmful mutations and cannot purge them efficiently. Recombination lets harmful mutations be separated from beneficial ones.
- Fisher-Muller: sex can combine beneficial mutations from different lineages.

Observationally, almost all asexual lineages are evolutionarily young, suggesting they accumulate problems and go extinct.
items.why: Sex's costs are enormous and obvious; its benefits are subtle and long-term. Evolution favours it anyway, and the reasons are still debated.

items.title: The oxygen you breathe comes from WATER, not CO2
items.claim: Photosynthesis takes in CO2 and water and produces sugar and oxygen. Every chemistry student writes the equation. But the O2 released is not stripped from the CO2 — it comes entirely from splitting water molecules.
items.prompt: How do we know the oxygen comes from water?

options.text: Both water and CO2 contribute oxygen equally
Ruben and Kamen (1941) used the heavy isotope oxygen-18 to label either water or CO2; the released O2 carried the label only when the water was labelled, never when the CO2 was
CO2 is the source of the oxygen

items.reveal:
The light reactions of photosynthesis split water (photolysis) at the oxygen-evolving complex — a manganese-calcium cluster in Photosystem II. Two water molecules are split: 2 H2O -> 4 H+ + 4 e- + O2.

The electrons enter the electron transport chain. The protons contribute to the thylakoid pH gradient (lumen reaches pH ~5, stroma ~8). ATP synthase uses the gradient to make ATP.

The Calvin cycle (in the stroma) uses ATP and NADPH to fix CO2 into sugar. The carbon from CO2 becomes the carbon in glucose. But the oxygen atoms in CO2 mostly end up in carbohydrate, NOT in the released O2.

Oxygen is, from photosynthesis's point of view, a waste product — and arguably the most consequential pollution event in Earth's history (the Great Oxidation Event, ~2.4 billion years ago, killed most anaerobic life).
items.why: The arrow-pushing equation suggests CO2 donates oxygen. The actual chemistry inverts that: water is split, CO2 is reduced, and the oxygen you breathe was once dissolved in a chloroplast.

items.title: Wounded plants warn their neighbours via airborne chemicals
items.claim: An acacia tree being browsed by giraffes releases volatile chemicals (methyl jasmonate, ethylene). Downwind acacias detect the signal and produce defensive tannins within 30 minutes — before any herbivore has reached them.

options.text: The signal probably evolved for systemic intra-plant communication (alerting other parts of the same tree); the inter-plant 'warning' is likely a by-product, though it does benefit kin or close neighbours under some conditions
Plants control each other's defences telepathically
It's a coincidence, not a signal

items.reveal_title: Volatile organic compounds in plant communication
items.reveal:
Wouter van Hoven (1980s) and Edward Farmer/Clarence Ryan (1990s) showed that plants under attack release volatile signals that other plants detect.

Mechanism: damaged tissue produces jasmonic acid; some is released as methyl jasmonate (volatile). Other plants take it in through stomata. It triggers expression of defensive genes — protease inhibitors that make leaves indigestible, tannins, alkaloids.

Other signals include green leaf volatiles (the smell of cut grass), terpenoids, ethylene. Each can trigger specific responses in receivers.

The original function is almost certainly within-plant: signalling from damaged leaves to undamaged ones via volatile leakage through the air, faster than through phloem in some cases. Lab tests show same-individual leaves respond as well as neighbours' leaves do.

Some plants also send volatile signals that attract predators of their herbivores. Maize plants attacked by caterpillars release blends specific to the caterpillar species, attracting parasitic wasps that lay eggs in the caterpillars.

'Crying plant' studies are controversial. Effect sizes vary by experiment, and the term 'warning' is anthropomorphic — but the chemistry is real, well-characterised, and has agricultural implications (push-pull pest management exploits these signals).
items.why: Plants seem passive. Volatile chemical signalling is widespread, sophisticated, and rich — and entire chemical 'languages' between plants and their herbivores and predators are still being decoded.
